en: In the *Peṭakopadesa*,
regarding the analysis of the suttas,
no prior limit is discerned for ignorance and the craving for existence.
In this regard, for beings who are hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, no prior limit is discerned.
Among them, those beings who are fettered by craving are full of attachment and weak in insight;
whereas those beings who have an abundance of views are abundant in insight and weak in attachment.
In this regard, beings of craving-temperament are obsessed by the perception of a self and do not see arising and passing away.
They regard the five aggregates as a self, thinking: "The self possesses form," or "form is in the self," or "the self is in form.
Thus it is with the five aggregates.
They regard the self as distinct from the other aggregates. Those beings with exaggerated views, while practicing insight, regard the aggregates directly as the self.
They regard form as the self:
"That which is form, that is the self."
He who says, "I am that form," sees the destruction of that form; he is an annihilationist.
Thus, from the initial impact upon the five aggregates, there are five views of self-identity that partake in annihilationism, namely: "The soul and the body are one and the same."
Regarding each individual aggregate, one clings to eternalism through the three latter terms, namely: "the soul is one thing, the body is another.
Outside of this [teaching], those who have gone forth and are of craving-temperament dwell devoted to the pursuit of sensual pleasure.
Through that same consequence, those of view-temperament dwell devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification.
By means of that very pleasure of view, the external application extends thus far.
In this regard, those beings of speculative temperament who enter the Noble Dhamma and Vinaya are followers by Dhamma (dhammānusārino).
Those beings of craving-temperament who enter the Noble Dhamma and Vinaya are followers by faith (saddhānusārino).

In that regard, those beings who are of a speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) hold a view of harm regarding sensual pleasures; yet, because their underlying tendencies toward sensual pleasures have not been eradicated, they dwell devoted to the pursuit of self-mortification.
To them the Teacher teaches the Dhamma—or another disciple [teaches it], saying:
"There is no benefit in sensual pleasures. Since they were already previously indifferent to sensual pleasures, they relinquish sensual pleasures without difficulty.
They are not obsessed by mental suffering;
therefore, it is called "the pleasant way of practice.
However, those beings who are dominated by craving are obsessed with sense pleasures; for them, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma.
Or another bhikkhu thinks, "There is no purpose in sensual pleasures," and they relinquish what is dear to them with difficulty.
Therefore, it is called "the painful way of practice.
Thus, all these beings converge upon two ways of practice: the painful and the pleasant.
In that regard, those beings who are of speculative temperament (diṭṭhicarita) are of two kinds: those with dull faculties (mudindriya) and those with sharp faculties (tikkhindriya).

Among them, those beings of speculative temperament who have sharp faculties relinquish [the hindrances] easily and realize [the path] quickly; therefore, it is called "the easy way with swift direct knowledge" (khippābhiññā sukhā paṭipadā).

Among them, those beings of speculative temperament who have dull faculties—being slower than those with sharp faculties to realize [the path]—relinquish [the hindrances] easily, yet they realize [the path] slowly.
Therefore it is said: "The pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge.
In that regard, beings of craving-disposition are of two kinds: those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties.
Among them, those beings of craving-disposition who have sharp faculties relinquish [the defilements] with difficulty, yet they realize [the goal] quickly.
Therefore it is said: "The painful practice with quick direct knowledge.

In that regard, those beings of craving-temperament who have dull faculties and realize [the goal] more slowly than those with sharp faculties first—since they relinquish with difficulty and realize slowly—it is therefore called "the painful practice with slow direct knowledge."
These are the four modes of practice, with no fifth and no sixth.
For whoever has attained extinction or will attain extinction, it is by means of these four modes of practice and no others; thus, by this tetrad of modes, he demonstrates the defilements.
That which is to be demonstrated among the noble states by way of the fourfold path is called the method known as the "Lion’s Play" (Sīhavikkīḷita).
In this regard, there are these four nutriments.
There are four perversions, clingings, yokes, ties, taints, floods, arrows, stations of consciousness, and ways of going to ruin—thus, all these ten terms [are included].
This is the coordination of the sutta.
There are four nutriments.
Among them, the nutriment of physical food and the nutriment of contact are to be abandoned by one of craving-temperament.
Among them, the nutriment of mental volition and the nutriment of consciousness are to be abandoned by one of view-temperament.
The first nutriment is the first perversion; the second nutriment is the second perversion; the third nutriment is the third perversion; the fourth nutriment is the fourth perversion.
These four perversions are without a fifth or a sixth.
And these, by way of measure, are the four nutriments.
Therein, one who stands in the first perversion clings to sense pleasures; this is clinging to sense pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
One who stands in the second perversion clings to future existence; this is clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*).
One who stands in the third perversion, being perverted, clings to views; this is clinging to views (*diṭṭhupādāna*).
Established in the fourth perversion, one clings to the aggregates as a self; this is the clinging to a doctrine of self (*attavādupādāna*).
Therein, established in the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*), one covets and is fettered by sense-pleasures; this is the bodily fetter of covetousness (*abhijjhākāyagantha*).
Established in the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*), one is fettered by ill-will; this is the bodily fetter of ill-will (*byāpādakāyagantha*).
Standing upon the clinging to views, one binds oneself through misapprehension; this is the bodily tie of misapprehension (*parāmāsa-kāyagantha*).

Standing upon the clinging to the doctrine of self, one binds oneself through conceptual proliferation; this is the bodily tie of dogmatic adherence to the notion "this alone is the truth" (*idamsaccābhinivesa-kāyagantha*).
Bound by these ties, the defilements flow out as taints (*āsava*).
Now, some say that remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) is what is meant;
those which are forms of remorse are the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*).

In this context, through the bodily tie of covetousness (*abhijjhā-kāyagantha*), there is the taint of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*); through the bodily tie of ill will (*byāpāda-kāyagantha*), the taint of existence (*bhavāsava*); through the bodily tie of dogmatic misapprehension (*parāmāsa-kāyagantha*), the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*); and through the bodily tie of adherence to "this alone is the truth" (*idaṃ-saccābhinivesa-kāyagantha*), there is the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
When those four taints have reached a state of abundance, they become floods; therefore, they are called "floods.

Therein, the taint of sensual desire is the flood of sensual desire, the taint of existence is the flood of existence, the taint of ignorance is the flood of ignorance, and the taint of views is the flood of views.
When those four floods have entered the underlying disposition and are accompanied by latent tendencies, they are so described.
"Remaining with arrows piercing the heart":

therein, the flood of sensual desire is the arrow of lust; the flood of existence is the arrow of hatred; the flood of ignorance is the arrow of delusion; and the flood of views is the arrow of wrong view.
Consciousness, gripped by these four arrows, remains fixed upon four things: form, feeling, perception, and mental formations.
These are the four stations of consciousness.
Therein, consciousness that has reached form stands, moistened by delight, with the dart of lust;

consciousness that has reached feeling stands with the dart of hatred; consciousness that has reached perception stands with the dart of delusion; and consciousness that has reached mental formations stands, moistened by delight, with the dart of views.
By means of the four stations of consciousness, beings go to the fourfold wrong course through desire, hatred, fear, and delusion.

Through desire, one goes to a wrong course by way of lust; through hatred, one goes to a wrong course by way of aversion; through delusion, one goes to a wrong course by way of confusion; and through views, one goes to a wrong course by way of fear.
Thus, this is both karma and these are the defilements.
This is the cause of saṃsāra.

In this regard, there are these four directions: edible food, the perversion of perceiving the foul as beautiful, clinging to sensual pleasures, the yoke of sensual pleasures, the bodily tie of covetousness, the taint of sensual pleasures, the flood of sensual pleasures, the dart of lust, the station of consciousness that leads to the realm of form, and going on a wrong path through desire.
This is the first direction.

Contact as nutriment, the perversion that there is happiness in what is suffering, clinging to rules and observances, the bond of existence, ill will, the bodily tie, the taint of existence, the flood of existence, the dart of hatred, the station for consciousness associated with feeling, and going on a bad path through hatred—

this is the second direction. Mental volition as nutriment, the perversion that there is a self in what is non-self, clinging to views, the bond of views, the bodily tie of misapprehension, the taint of views, the flood of views, the dart of views, the station for consciousness associated with perception, and going on a bad path through fear— this is the third direction.

The nutriment of consciousness (*viññāṇāhāra*), the perversion of taking what is impermanent as permanent, the clinging to a self-doctrine, the bond of ignorance, the adherence to the view "this is the truth," the bodily tie,
the taint of ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the dart of delusion, the station for consciousness that leads toward formations, and the going on a wrong path due to delusion—
this is the fourth direction. Thus, by the first word of these ten discourses, there is the illumination of the first direction.
This is called "surveying the directions.

Surveying the directions on the side of the unwholesome through the four perversions (vipallāsas) while binding oneself to defilement—this is the ground for surveying the directions on the side of the unwholesome.
Regarding the first words of the five or ten suttas, what is the meaning of these phenomena?
The meaning is one; only the phrasing is different.
Thus for the second, thus for the third, thus for the fourth.
This is the first correlation.
By this same method, all defilements are to be included within these four categories.
Then, on the side of the wholesome, there are the four ways of practice, the four jhānas, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four abodes— divine,
brahma-like, noble, and imperturbable— the four right efforts, and the four wonderful and marvelous qualities.
There are four foundations, which are concentrations: concentration of desire, concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of investigation.

There are four things conducive to happiness: nothing other than the factors of enlightenment, nothing other than austerity, nothing other than restraint of the faculties, and nothing other than the relinquishment of everything—namely, the four immeasurables.
Therein, when the painful practice with slow direct knowledge is being developed and cultivated, it leads to the first *jhāna*.
It fulfills it; the fulfilled first jhāna fulfills the first foundation of mindfulness;
the fulfilled first foundation of mindfulness fulfills the first abiding;
the fulfilled first abiding fulfills the first right exertion; the fulfilled first right exertion fulfills the first marvel.
He fulfills the wonderful quality; the first wonderful and marvelous quality fulfilled fulfills the first foundation;
the first foundation fulfilled fulfills concentration through desire; concentration through desire fulfilled fulfills restraint of the faculties;
restraint of the faculties fulfilled fulfills the first immeasurable state of loving-kindness.
In this way, up to the relinquishment of everything fulfills the fourth immeasurable.
Therein, the first way of practice, the first jhāna, the first foundation of mindfulness, the first abiding, the first right exertion,
the first wonderful and marvelous phenomenon, and the foundation of truth— these are fulfilled.
Concentration through zeal, restraint of the sense faculties, and immeasurable loving-kindness— this is the first direction.
The painful practice with swift direct knowledge, the second jhāna, the second foundation of mindfulness, and the second [supernormal power]— [this is the second direction].
The dwelling, the second right effort, the second wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of generosity, mental concentration,
the four bases of psychic power, and the immeasurable compassion— this is the second direction.
The pleasant way of practice with sluggish direct knowledge, the third jhāna, the third foundation of mindfulness, and the third...
The dwelling, the third right exertion, the third wonderful and marvelous quality, the foundation of wisdom,
energy-concentration, the awakening factors, and the immeasurable joy—
this is the third direction.
The pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge, the fourth jhāna, the fourth foundation of mindfulness,
the fourth abiding, the fourth right exertion, the fourth wonderful and marvelous quality,
the basis of tranquility, the concentration of investigation, the relinquishment of all, equanimity, and the immeasurable.
This is the fourth direction.
This is the illumination of these four directions.
This is called the method known as "Illumination of the Directions."
Herein, this is the application:
the four nutriments and the four ways of practice; the four perversions and the four foundations of mindfulness;
the four clingings and the four jhānas; the four bonds and the four abidings; the ties and the four right efforts.
The taints and the wonderful, marvelous qualities; the floods and the foundations; the arrows and the concentrations;
the stations of consciousness and the four states conducive to happiness;

the four ways of going to ruin and the four immeasurables—this is the application by way of the opposites of the wholesome and the unwholesome. This is called the method of "Illumination of the Directions."
For him, the four fruits of asceticism are the conclusion; and as for the first section on directions in the exposition of wholesome and unwholesome states,
the fruit of stream-entry is its conclusion, the second is the fruit of once-returning,
the third is the fruit of non-returning, and the fourth is the fruit of arahantship.
In this regard, what is the Tipukkhalo method?

There are two types of persons who go forth by means of the painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge and those who go forth by means of the painful practice with swift direct knowledge; and there are two types of persons who go forth by means of the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge and those who go forth by means of the pleasant practice with swift direct knowledge.

Among these four types of persons, it is the person who goes forth by means of the pleasant practice with sluggish direct knowledge and the person who goes forth by means of the painful practice with swift direct knowledge.
There are these two types of persons.
Among them, he who goes forth by means of the pleasant way with swift direct knowledge is one who understands through a condensed presentation (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
He who is the latter person, who is common to both ways, is one who understands through an expanded exposition (*vipañcitaññū*).
The person who proceeds by means of sluggish direct knowledge and a painful way of practice is one who is to be led (*neyya*).

These four types, when condensed, become three; therein, for one who knows by a condensed teaching (*ugghaṭitaññū*), insight is preceded by serenity; for one who is to be led, serenity is preceded by insight; and for one who knows by an elaborated teaching (*vipañcitaññū*), serenity and insight are coupled together.
For one who knows by a condensed teaching, the teaching is gentle; for one who is to be led, the teaching is sharp; for one who knows by an elaborated teaching, the teaching is both sharp and gentle.

For one who understands through a condensed teaching, there is the training in higher wisdom; for one who is to be led, there is the training in higher mind; for one who understands through an expanded teaching, there is the training in higher virtue.
Thus, for these types of persons, there is deliverance by way of four modes of practice.

In this regard, this is the corruption: the three unwholesome roots, the three kinds of contact, the three kinds of feeling, the three kinds of mental exploration, the three corruptions, the three kinds of thought, the three fevers, the three characteristics of the conditioned, and the three kinds of suffering.
The three unwholesome roots are: greed as an unwholesome root, hatred as an unwholesome root, and delusion as an unwholesome root.
The three types of contact are: contact to be experienced as pleasant, contact to be experienced as painful, and contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
The three feelings are: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

There are three modes of mental application: the mode of mental application associated with joy, the mode of mental application associated with grief, and the mode of mental application associated with equanimity.
There are three defilements: lust, hatred, and delusion.
There are three types of thought: sensual thought, ill-will thought, and cruelty thought.
The three fevers are those born of lust, those born of hatred, and those born of delusion.
The three characteristics of the conditioned are arising, persistence, and passing away.
The three kinds of suffering are the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of the conditioned.
In that regard, from what does the unwholesome root of greed arise?
There are three kinds of objects: the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is a basis for equanimity.
Among these, the unwholesome root of greed arises by means of an agreeable object.
Thus, there is a pleasant object; contact to be experienced as pleasant arises; dependent on contact to be experienced as pleasant, a feeling to be experienced as pleasant arises;
dependent on a feeling to be experienced as pleasant, an investigation accompanied by joy arises; dependent on an investigation accompanied by joy, lust arises;
dependent on lust, sensual thought arises; dependent on sensual thought...
The fever born of lust arises; dependent on the fever born of lust, there arises arising, which is a conditioned characteristic;
dependent on arising, the conditioned characteristic, there arises the suffering of change.
From what does hatred, the unwholesome root, arise?
Through an unpleasant object, hatred—the unwholesome root—arises.
Thus, from an unpleasant object arises contact to be felt as painful; dependent on contact to be felt as painful, a painful feeling arises;
dependent on a painful feeling, a mental exploration accompanied by displeasure arises; [dependent on] the mental exploration accompanied by displeasure...
Dependent on anger, hatred arises; dependent on hatred, thoughts of ill will arise; dependent on thoughts of ill will, fever born of hatred arises;
dependent on fever born of hatred, the characteristic of the conditioned—the alteration of that which stands—arises;
and dependent on the characteristic of the conditioned—the alteration of that which stands—the feeling of the suffering of suffering arises.
From what does the unwholesome root of delusion arise?
The unwholesome root of delusion arises from an object that is a basis for equanimity.
Thus, from objects that are a basis for equanimity comes contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant; [and] the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling...
Dependent on contact, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises; dependent on neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity-investigation arises;
dependent on equanimity-investigation, delusion arises; dependent on delusion, a thought of cruelty arises;
dependent on a thought of cruelty, a fever born of delusion arises. Dependent on the fever born of delusion...
Dependent upon the characteristic of the conditioned, passing away arises; dependent upon the characteristic of the conditioned, passing away, the state of suffering in the conditioned arises.
Thus, this is the exposition of the three defilements; this is called the "three-pointed method" on the side of the wholesome.

Thus, there are three unwholesome roots—neither a fourth nor a fifth—and three types of contact, three feelings, and so on up to the state of suffering in the conditioned: whatever belongs to the side of the unwholesome, all that converges within the three unwholesome roots.
In this regard, what is the side of the wholesome?
The three roots of the wholesome; the three kinds of wisdom: wisdom consisting of hearing, wisdom consisting of reflection, and wisdom consisting of cultivation;
and the three concentrations: with applied thought and sustained thought, [and so forth].
The three trainings: the training in higher virtue … [and so on] … the training.
The three signs: the sign of calm, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity.
Three types of thought: the thought of renunciation … [and so on] … the thought of non-harming.
Three faculties: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," and so forth in detail.
There are three modes of conduct: the mode of conduct of renunciation, the mode of conduct of non-ill will, and the mode of conduct of non-cruelty.
There are three searches: the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life.
There are three aggregates: the aggregate of virtue, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
In this regard, that which is the root of wholesome merit—non-greed—fulfills wisdom consisting in what has been heard;

wisdom consisting in what has been heard, when fulfilled, fulfills concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought; concentration accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, when fulfilled, fulfills the training in higher consciousness;
the training in higher consciousness, when fulfilled, fulfills the sign of serenity. The sign of serenity...
The fulfilled thought of renunciation fulfills the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown";
the fulfilled faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" fulfills the investigation of renunciation;
the fulfilled investigation of renunciation abandons the search for sensual pleasures; and the abandonment of the search for sensual pleasures fulfills the aggregate of concentration.
Non-hatred, as a root of the wholesome, fulfills wisdom born of reflection; wisdom born of reflection, when fulfilled, fulfills concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought.
Concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought, when fulfilled, fulfills the training in higher virtue;
the training in higher virtue, when fulfilled, fulfills the sign of equanimity; the sign of equanimity, when fulfilled, fulfills thoughts of non-ill will.
It fulfills it; the fulfilled thought of non-ill will fulfills the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*); the fulfilled faculty of final knowledge fulfills the investigation of non-ill will;
the fulfilled investigation of non-ill will abandons the search for existence; the abandonment of the search for existence fulfills the aggregate of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*).

Non-delusion, as a root of the wholesome, fulfills wisdom consisting in development; wisdom consisting in development, when fulfilled, fulfills concentration without applied thought and sustained thought;
concentration without applied thought and sustained thought, when fulfilled, fulfills the training in higher wisdom;
the training in higher wisdom, when fulfilled, fulfills the sign of exertion; the sign of exertion, when fulfilled—
The faculty of one who has final knowledge fulfills the faculty of one who has final knowledge; the faculty of one who has final knowledge, when fulfilled, fulfills the investigation of non-harming;
the investigation of non-harming, when fulfilled, fulfills the search for the holy life; the search for the holy life, when fulfilled, fulfills the aggregate of wisdom.
Thus, these three states belonging to the side of the wholesome—namely, all wholesome states—are demonstrated by means of three triplets; the three gateways to liberation constitute their conclusion.
Therein, by the first [triplet] the wishless (*appaṇihita*) is shown, by the second the void (*suññata*), and by the third the signless (*animitta*).
This is called the second method, known as "the Threefold Array" (*tipukkhalo*).

In this context, regarding these three types of persons—the one who gains knowledge by a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*), the one who gains knowledge by an elaborated explanation (*vipañcitaññū*), and the one who is led to understanding (*neyya*)—among these three, those persons who proceed by way of the pleasant path with quick direct knowledge and by way of the pleasant path with sluggish direct knowledge constitute two types of persons.

Furthermore, those two persons who proceed by way of the painful path with quick direct knowledge and by way of the painful path with sluggish direct knowledge—these four, distinguished by that [difference], become two: the one characterized by views (*diṭṭhicarita*) and the one characterized by craving (*taṇhācarita*).
These four, having become so, become three; these three, having become so, become two.

For these two types of persons, this is the defilement: ignorance and craving, moral shamelessness and lack of moral dread, lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension, the hindrances and the fetters, and attachment and dogmatic adherence.

Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamaṅkāra*), lack of faith (*assaddhiya*) and difficult-to-correctness (*dovacassa*), laziness (*kosajja*) and improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), doubt (*vicikicchā*) and covetousness (*abhijjhā*),
hearing what is not the true Dhamma (*asaddhammassavana*) and non-attainment (*asamāpatti*).

In this context, ignorance (*avijjā*), moral shamelessness (*ahirika*), lack of mindfulness (*assati*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), attachment (*ajjhosāna*), egoism, lack of faith, laziness, doubt, and hearing what is not the true Dhamma— this is one direction.

Craving, lack of moral dread, lack of clear comprehension, fetters, dogmatic adherence, the sense of "mine," difficult-to-correctness, improper attention, covetousness, and failure to attain concentration—this is the second direction.
For the ten dyads, the first ten terms should be formulated.
They indicate the meaning in brief; for all the dyads, the second terms refer to the opposing dark side—this is the second direction.
Thus is the exposition of suffering regarding unwholesome states; this is the origin.

That which dwells upon these phenomena—namely, name-and-form—is suffering; thus, both this origin and this suffering constitute two truths: suffering and its origin. This is the first exposition in the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.
In that regard, what is the side of the wholesome?
Tranquility and insight; true knowledge and conduct; mindfulness and clear comprehension; moral shame and moral dread;
the abandoning of the conceit "I am" and the abandoning of the conceit "mine"; right effort and wise attention;
right mindfulness and right concentration; wisdom and disenchantment; meditative attainment and hearing the true Dhamma; and joy.
And the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Therein, serenity, true knowledge, mindfulness, moral shame, the abandoning of the conceit "I am," right effort, right mindfulness, wisdom, meditative attainment, and mental joy—these factors constitute one direction.
Insight, conduct, clear comprehension, moral dread, the abandoning of the conceit "mine," and wise attention [constitute the other].
Right concentration, disenchantment, hearing the true Dhamma, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma—this is the second direction.
Thus, regarding both the side of the wholesome and the side of the unwholesome, there are four directions in the Nandiyāvaṭṭa method.

Among them, those unwholesome factors which are the first terms on the side of the unwholesome and which are abandoned by means of the wholesome, are abandoned by means of the second terms on the side of the wholesome.

With their abandoning, through the fading away of lust, there is liberation of mind; those second unwholesome factors on the side of the unwholesome which undergo abandoning do so by means of the first factors on the side of the wholesome.
With their abandoning, through the fading away of ignorance, there is liberation by wisdom as the culmination.
Of these three methods, the first method is called the "Lion’s Play."
Eight terms—four wholesome and four unwholesome—are these eight root terms; according to the method of meaning, this is the second, the Tipukkhalo.

It leads by way of six factors: it leads the wholesome roots and the unwholesome roots. Thus, these six terms together with the preceding eight root terms make these fourteen terms for the eighteen root terms.
Therein, the latter method, the Nandiyāvaṭṭa, leads by way of four factors.
By means of ignorance and craving, and by means of serenity and insight—these four states and these eighteen root-terms are demonstrated in three methods.
Therein, as for the nine terms that are wholesome, all that is wholesome converges therein.
Of those nine roots, four terms are in the "Lion’s Play" method, three in the "Three Cycles" method, and two in the "Joyful Turn" method; these are the sides of the wholesome.
In that regard, among those nine terms which are wholesome, everything wholesome is applicable there.
Among them, four terms are indicated as wholesome in the *Sīhavikkīḷita* method, three in the *Tipukkhalo*, and two in the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa*; thus these nine terms are shown to be wholesome.
Among those four terms in the *Nandiyāvaṭṭa* method, eighteen root-terms converge there.
How so? Tranquility, non-greed, non-hatred, the perception of foulness, and the perception of suffering—these five factors on the side of the wholesome belong to tranquility (*samatha*).
Insight, non-delusion, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of non-self—these four factors belong to insight (*vipassanā*).
These nine wholesome factors are thus applied to two categories. In that regard, concerning the nine unwholesome root-factors on the side of the unwholesome:
Craving, greed, hatred, the perception of beauty, and the perception of pleasure—
these five terms belong to craving.
Ignorance, delusion, the perception of permanence, and the perception of self— these four terms belong to ignorance.
These nine unwholesome terms are well condensed.
Thus, three methods do not enter into a single method.
In this way, the eighteen root terms are to be demonstrated according to the "Joyous Turn" (Nandiyāvaṭṭa) method.
How do the eighteen root-terms apply to the method of the three cycles?
Of the nine wholesome terms, there are these four terms: insight, non-delusion, the perception of impermanence, and the perception of non-self;
and there are these four terms: non-delusion, serenity, non-greed, and the perception of foulness.
Greed and hatred—thus these nine terms are to be applied to the three unwholesome roots.
Among those nine unwholesome terms, craving, greed, the perception of beauty, and the perception of pleasure—these four terms constitute greed as an unwholesome root.
Ignorance, delusion, the perception of permanence, and the perception of self—this is delusion, this is hatred. And these are the nine terms that have been applied to the three unwholesome roots.
Thus, having applied the eighteen root-terms to the roots of the wholesome, they are to be demonstrated by means of the "Threefold Array" method (*tipukkhalanaya*).
How do the eighteen root-terms apply to the "Lion's Play" method (*sīhavikkīḷitanaya*)?
Craving and the perception of beauty—this is the first perversion.
Greed and the perception of pleasure—this is the second perversion.
Ignorance and the perception of permanence—this is the third perversion.
Delusion and the perception of self—this is the fourth perversion.
Thus, nine terms, which are the roots of unwholesomeness, are applied to four bases.
Therein, among the nine root-terms, both the wholesome *samatha* and the perception of foulness (*asubha-saññā*) constitute the first foundation of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Both non-greed (*alobha*) and the perception of suffering (*dukkha-saññā*) constitute the second foundation of mindfulness.
Insight and the perception of impermanence: this is the third foundation of mindfulness.
Non-delusion and the perception of non-self: this is the fourth foundation of mindfulness.
These eighteen root terms have entered into the method of the lion’s sport.
Of these three methods, whatever the plane, whatever the lust, and whatever the hatred, they enter into one method.

When the unwholesome or wholesome states of one method have been understood, the counteragent must be sought; having sought the counteragent, that method is to be demonstrated as it has been demonstrated within that method.
Just as all methods are included within one method, so should they be demonstrated.
In one method, eighteen root-terms are included; when that Dhamma is understood, all Dhammas are understood.
Of these three methods, the conclusion of the Lion’s Play method consists of four fruits:
the first fruit is in the first direction, the second fruit is in the second direction, the third fruit is in the third direction, and the fourth fruit is in the fourth direction.
The conclusion of the Tipukkhalo method consists of the three gateways to liberation:
the wishless (appaṇihita) for the first direction, the void (suññatā) for the second direction, and the signless (animitta) for the third direction.
The conclusion of the Nandiāvatto method is the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust (rāgavirāga) and the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance (avijjāvirāga).
In the first direction there is liberation of mind through the fading away of lust; in the second direction there is liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.
These three methods are the illumination of these three methods' eighteen root-terms; this is called the method of the illumination of directions.
Having illuminated them, one knows: "This state belongs to that state"—this is right application.
This method applies both to the side of the wholesome and to the side of the unwholesome; it is called the "hook.
These are the five methods.
Regarding this, here is the summary verse:
Craving and ignorance,
greed, hatred, and likewise delusion,
and the four perversions.
The nine sections on the plane of defilements;
and the foundations of mindfulness,
serenity, insight, and the roots of the wholesome.
All this is wholesome;
the stage of the faculties consists of nine terms.
All that is wholesome is connected with these nine terms.
And the nine unwholesome [roots];
these are the root-terms,
eighteen terms in both cases.
Craving and ignorance,
serenity and insight— he who leads [the path],
yoked to all [these], is the one [to be known].
This method is the "Joyous Turn" (nandiyāvaṭṭa).
That which is led by wholesome roots— by both wholesome and unwholesome roots;
It is real, true, and not false;
they call that the Tipukkhala method.
He leads away from the perversions.
And with the defilements and the faculties;
they call that method of guiding the phenomena the "Lion’s Play."
When the exposition has been spoken,
through skillful and unskillful qualities,
he illuminates three things.
This method is called "orienting the directions.
Having observed with the orienting of the directions,
one sets down [the object] and brings it into alignment.
"All wholesome and unwholesome states"—
this method is called the "hook.
This concludes the section on the arising of methods.
In the *Peṭakopadesa*, the Elder Mahākaccāyana’s exposition of the analysis of the discourses (*suttavibhaṅga*) is completed.
Those fourfold sets, both unwholesome and wholesome, which were demonstrated in the *Sīhavikkīḷita* method, as well as the threefold sets that are wholesome...
Furthermore, the unwholesome [factors] are demonstrated in the Tipukkhalanaya method; the dyads of both wholesome and unwholesome [factors] are demonstrated in the Nandiyāvaṭṭanaya method.

Regarding those two types of phenomena that are wholesome, when they are analyzed within the triplets, there is the plane of existence (*bhavabhūmi*); moreover, the entire meaning is demonstrated by means of three expressions.
That much is said.
That meaning which cannot be demonstrated by means of four terms and twenty-eight divisions—that very meaning he demonstrates while moving within those four terms.
Thus, the non-exceeding of what has been demonstrated in this way is the measure.

Just as all concentrations are to be sought within the three concentrations—namely, with applied thought and sustained thought, without applied thought and with sustained thought only, and without applied thought and without sustained thought—this is the measure; there is no fourth concentration.
Likewise, the three kinds of wisdom—consisting of reflection, consisting of hearing, and consisting of cultivation—are indicated among all forms of wisdom;
there is no fourth wisdom that does not consist of reflection, hearing, or cultivation.
That wisdom which exists for these phenomena as non-distraction is called "measure."
The *Peṭakopadesa* of the Elder Mahākaccāyana, dweller of the Rose-apple Grove, is completed.
The treatise *Peṭakopadesa* is finished.
